content:
The old well sat at the tail of the village, dry for twenty years. Moss lay thick on the stone rim, thick enough to wring water from, and when the wind passed, a fishy reek climbed up the well-rope, as if someone below had turned over in his sleep and shaken loose the damp of decades. By day the sun could not reach through; the mouth of the well was always in shadow, like a half-closed eye watching the villagers come and go.

The villagers walked around the well. Those who came for water came only before dawn, filled their buckets, and left at a quick step; no one would linger by the rim. The old said this well was where, years ago, the town's condemned had been sunk, their bodies left unrecovered so the well opened onto the underworld. Others said a thing lived at the bottom that collected guilty secrets — whatever you threw in that could not bear the light, it kept for you, kept it until the day it demanded you go down yourself to settle the account. Shen heard that as a joke in his youth; now, sitting there at night, every word seemed spoken to him alone.

The well-keeper's surname was Shen; everyone called him Old Shen, and his given name no one remembered, no one asked. He had kept this well for thirty full years. In those years the rope was replaced seven times, the bucket three, the iron lock on the rim five, and the lock's tongue bore the print of his grip. His task was simple to name: by day he locked the rim; by night he sat by the well with the polished rope, listening to the wind. Listening to the bucket creak in the night air, listening for any wrong sound from below. The villagers feared the well; they said its bottom opened onto the underworld, and whoever threw himself in would have his soul sink down the water-veins and never return. Old Shen's task was to stop them.

How he became the well-keeper even he could not say. Thirty years before, he had been a man of the yamen who offended his superiors and was sent back to the village to watch this well everyone shunned. At first he found it unlucky; in time he grew used to it. The old locust by the well he had planted when he came; now two men could not span its trunk. Each evening at dusk he came out with his lantern, checked the locks on the rim one by one, then settled on the rope and smoked pipe after pipe until the east turned pale. The villagers called him dutiful; only he knew he guarded not the well, but the things he had thrown in and feared someone might fish back out.

He had stopped a widow who came to throw herself in, a woman who wept all night by the well with an empty bundle in her arms; he sat three paces off and said nothing, only watched. He had stopped a young man who lost at dice and loosed his belt to jump; he flung himself on the cloth and gripped it white at the knuckles. He had stopped a drunk at the Dragon-Boat festival who reeled toward the mouth; the drunk cursed him for meddling, and he let the curses fall while his hand on the rope never loosened. The lock was broken three times, each time by his own wrenching — he would rather break the lock than let a single soul down.

One Dragon-Boat festival a village lad drank two bowls of realgar wine too many and insisted on peering into the well to see what the underworld looked like. Shen hauled him back and slapped him, cursing his lack of sense. The lad covered his face and wept, saying he had heard a woman singing a nursery tune softly from the well, the tune from the year of the great drought. Shen's hand froze in mid-air and did not fall again. He did not yet know it, but what the lad heard need not have been illusion. The throat at the bottom had long been trying its voice; it simply had not yet reached the point of reciting his name.

Yet he would say in private that the one who most needed stopping was never another.

His own affairs, he had thrown into the well, one by one.

The first was tainted silver. That year he was a low runner in the town yamen, assisting the magistrate's clerk in a theft case on East Street. The true thief had long since fled, but a mute had been bound before the bench as a stand-in, dragged in from elsewhere to fill the count. The mute could not plead; he only knelt, forehead knocking the blue stone, knocking it red. The clerk took thirty taels of snowflake silver from the household and bade Shen write the mute down as the culprit and close the file. Shen had just entered the yamen, still raw from the countryside, and dared not refuse; yet he tossed all night, and at last drew the thirty taels from beneath the file and hid them in his own breast. The silver was heavy, pressing at his chest; he dared not keep it, dared not spend it — to spend was to bare the bottom. On the third night, in the thick black, he loosed the cloth that wrapped it, crouched at the mouth, made sure no one was near, and with a flick of the wrist threw it down. The mouth swallowed the thing without a sound, like a closing mouth, without even an echo. He laid his ear to the rim for a long while; below was black and still, nothing there.

Those thirty taels he never dared spend, never dared fish back up. Some nights he dreamed the mute kneeling before the bench, the red on his forehead pressing patch by patch onto Shen's own face; he would start awake and grope his way to the well, thrust his hand into the mouth to feel whether the wrapped silver was still there. The chill climbed his fingers and was gone, and he touched nothing. He told himself the thing was heavy and had long since reached the bottom. Yet it never occurred to him that a dry well has no bottom — what falls in need not stop.

The second was a wrongful verdict. The Zhao family's daughter on the east end had drowned in the pond; when they pulled her up, she still clutched half a length of red cord, the end snapped, darkened by the water. The Zhaos swore it was the cowherd A-Niu from the west end who did it, saying they had seen him go to the pond that day. A-Niu was a mute gourd who could only shake his head when pressed, who could not get out a whole sentence. When the case came to Shen, he was already a secretary who could speak before the clerk. He should have traced whose red cord it was, should have asked which household's drying line had snapped, should have asked whom the girl had seen the day before she died. He had in fact asked: the washerwoman by the pond said a stranger had indeed stood there half a morning, neatly dressed, no villager. He should have followed that thread; but halfway through his questioning the household's man arrived, pressed into his hand that sum of settling-silver, begging only that the matter be closed quickly and draw no other entanglements. Shen weighed the pouch, thought of the red jacket his new wife had worn through the door, thought of standing firm in the town hereafter, and swallowed the question that had reached his lips. So he wrote A-Niu's name into the confession. A-Niu knelt in the snow; three winters passed before, on a frosted morning, he hung himself from the crooked willow by the Zhao pond. The rope was re-twisted well-rope, and Shen knew the twist. Afterward he rolled the false confession into an old clay jar and threw that into the well, too. The jar fell, again without sound.

After A-Niu died, no one went to heap earth at the crooked willow by the Zhao pond, year after year at the graveside festival. Once Shen passed and saw the bare crooked willow; when the wind blew, the paper money hung on its branches rustled, as if someone answered from below. His chest tightened. Back in the village he read again the draft of A-Niu's confession; the words were his, the fingerprint A-Niu's — and when it was pressed, A-Niu's fingers had been purple with cold, unable to mark it for the longest time. He closed the file and stuffed it into the stove; the flame licked those few lines, and with a crackle it was as if A-Niu sighed. But the draft burned; the true copy had gone down with the clay jar the day he threw it in.

The third, heaviest, was poisoning. That year a great drought left the riverbed bare, and the whole village drew its water from this old well at the village's tail. The Zhou family's daughter-in-law had put arsenic in her mother-in-law's food, half a bowl of thin congee, the poison sinking to the bottom as it cooled. The mother-in-law died strangely, face bruised blue; the Zhou man came to the yamen beating the drum for justice. Shen examined the body; lifting the straw mat, he saw at once the poison was in the congee, the tongue blackened — arsenic, no doubt. But the daughter-in-law's family were distant kin to the newly posted judge. The judge sent word: should this case be aired, the daughter-in-law's family would lose face, but small beside it, Shen's own post as secretary would likely not survive. The word carried another meaning — handle it well, and there would be favor before the judge. That night he tore the autopsy slip by the oil lamp and wrote another: "sudden illness, natural death," and sent it back. The daughter-in-law never went to prison; the mother-in-law was buried in haste, not even a decent coffin, only a thin wooden box carried to the mass grave.

Having closed those three matters, Shen found his footing in the town; the secretary's seat sat steady under him. He took a new wife, fathered a son, and the days passed; the three things thrown into the well were pressed day by day into the darkest corner of his heart. He thought that so long as no one spoke of them, so long as the well stayed dry, those affairs had rotted in the well. He even gradually forgot the red on the mute's forehead, A-Niu's purple-cold fingers, the mother-in-law's blue-black face — remembered only that he was a dutiful well-keeper, guarding a dead well that gave no water.

These three matters he had thrown into the well one by one, like pressing stones into a deep pool, and once pressed, counted them gone. He thought the dry well bottomless, and what he threw in was buried. But the well was dry, and a dry well does not swallow sound.

For the first few years the bottom was quiet; the wind passed the rope, creaked twice, and was done. Yet when Shen sat by the well at night, the bucket seemed heavier than before, and when he lifted it, the bottom seemed to carry something he could not name, damp and dragging at his hand. He shook it; it would not shake off. The years went by; the moss by the well turned green then withered, withered then green. Shen's hair was more than half white, his back bent, yet the well was the same well, and the creak of the bucket in the wind had not changed a fraction. He began to sense something wrong: an ordinary dry well, after so many years, should have its wall cave in, should fill with earth — but the depths of this well were always empty, emptily unsettling, as if someone below had deliberately caught whatever fell and cleared space for more.

A few years more, and he heard an echo from below. Not wind, not water — a human voice, muffled, as if reciting something through three feet of wet earth. He pressed close to the rim to listen, and what he heard was plainly his own affair.

The voice recited very slowly, measure by measure, as if afraid he would not hear, or as if it meant him to suffer it one word at a time. It did not scold, did not plead, did not cry injustice; it only set out, flat and plain, the years, the names, the sums, one by one, cooler than any trial in the yamen. Shen listened, and thought the cadence faintly familiar — it was exactly the tone he himself had used reciting confessions before the bench. Only then did he grow afraid: the one reciting below, had he not learned Shen's whole life by heart?

First the thirty taels. On a night of frost's descent, someone below recited, word by word; the voice was an old man's, hoarse, without a trace of feeling, like reading an old account: East Street theft, the mute died in his place, thirty taels of silver, taken to Shen's breast, thrown into the well by night. Every hair on Shen's body rose; he crushed his pipe out on the sole of his shoe, the bowl knocking a fine sound. He told himself it was wind, a stone fallen from the wall and ringing, night dew dripping into the empty bucket. But the second night the voice came again, reciting the Zhao girl's matter: half a red cord, A-Niu wronged, one confession rolled, thrown into the well in snow. The third night, the Zhou daughter-in-law: year of great drought, half a bowl of arsenic congee, the autopsy slip changed to sudden death, thrown into the well by night.

One by one, the man below turned his old affairs back out, not one omitted. When it came to the Zhou matter, the voice paused a long while, so long Shen thought it tired, or had forgotten the rest. Yet at last it spoke, slower than before, each word pulled from wet earth with the sound of water: the mother-in-law blue-black, the thin wooden box, the mass grave, no one to gather the bones. Shen heard it clear. That matter he had pressed deepest, not even in his cups daring to think it. What the well recited, word for word, was the old case he had buried half his life; even the wrapping cloth for the silver, the clay jar for the confession, the altered autopsy slip — all set out plainly, as if below the well stood an acquaintance who had turned out the bottom of his chest, laying his darkest debts one by one into the light.

He began to be afraid. At night he dared not light a lamp; by lamplight the rope's shadow writhed on the wall, as if someone were climbing out of the well. He tried dropping stones to block the voice; the stones fell without a sound, as if into a pile of cotton, softly gone. He tried moving a millstone to seal the mouth, a stonecutter's work, very heavy; he panted to set it in place. But at dawn the millstone lay askew, and the rim's moss was wet in a ring, as if someone had pushed it open in the night and wiped a hand across. He crouched to study the wet ring; the prints were blurred, impossible to count.

He tried building a pile of mugwort by the well, thinking to smoke the voice back down; the fire jumped all night, the smoke made him cough, yet the voice from below came through the haze, not one word off. He tried pouring water into the well, thinking that once it filled it might cover the mouth below; but the water fell silent and the well stayed dry, as if the thing below could swallow water too. All he could do was clamp his ears, yet the voice came up through the wall itself, and plugging his ears only made it clearer, as if someone pressed against his skull to recite.

Once, unable to bear it, he said quietly to the mouth that those matters were years gone, the mute and A-Niu and the mother-in-law long dead — who, reciting this, would still know them? The instant he finished, the well answered with one phrase, still in that hoarse tone: I know. Shen's knees went soft on the spot; he clutched the rim to keep from sitting down. Only then did he understand: what the bottom recited was never for another's ear, but for his alone, and it would not be done until the day he heard it himself and confessed it himself.

The wind still came every night. Night wind swept the rim and lifted the fishy reek; the bucket creaked in the empty well, once, and once, as if the man below were also counting something — counting the few things he had thrown down, counting the lives he owed. Shen laid his ear to the cold wall and heard his own heartbeat, and another, slower and heavier, rising from the earth, the two laid one over the other, impossible to tell apart.

The night it recited the last matter, the rain was light but cold to the bone, the slanting threads beating the rim and making the moss wetter, brighter. Below, it finished the Zhou poisoning and did not stop as before, but paused and took a breath, as if the reader had turned to the last page.

Then a hand reached out of the well.

Not a shadow, not his eyes playing tricks, not a shape blurred from night mist. A gray-white hand, the knuckles swollen from soaking, the flesh hanging loose over bone, probing out of the wet moss at the mouth, resting on the rim, reaching slowly toward Shen. Below the wrist was bottomless dark, as if the hand had swum up from the well's bottom — swum thirty years to reach the rim. It did not grasp the rail; it only opened its palm upward, as if demanding something, or inviting him down, to speak face to face with the man below.

The voice from the bottom spoke then, still the hoarse old man, but now it recited Shen's name, measure by measure: Shen, come down, answer for it.

The wind stopped. The bucket was silent. The whole well was so still he could hear water-drops falling on the moss, drip, drip, as if the man below were counting the time he had left. The hand rested on the rim, palm up, unmoving, waiting.

Shen stared at that hand, and his mind churned with the three old matters: the mute's red forehead, A-Niu's purple-cold fingers, the mother-in-law's blue-black face, layering one over another until he could not breathe. The voice below urged once more: come down. His feet seemed nailed to the ground; half a step forward was the black mouth, half a step back was the living day, yet in the living days from then on, every night this hand would wait. He opened his mouth to say something, but his throat seemed stopped with the well's chill, and not half a word would come.

Shen stepped back one pace; his sole crushed a patch of dead moss by the well, the fragments clinging to his cloth shoe with a very faint rustle. He dared not answer, dared not run. For thirty years he had stopped others from throwing themselves in, lock after lock worn through, and in the end the one who must go down was himself. He looked at that hand; the veins stood on its back like the marks of well-rope, the same as on his own.

He did not go down. That night he sat by the well, back against the old locust, and watched the hand withdraw slowly from the rim, joint by joint, as if reluctant, as if with no choice. As it withdrew, it left five wet bright prints on the moss — five, no more no less — as if the man below, on leaving, had pressed his mark upon Shen, sealed the account, and acknowledged the debt.

He stared at those five prints for a long while; they were wet, and close up he could smell the well's fishy reek, the same as when he drew water by day. He reached to touch, and just as his fingertip neared, the chill slipped in past the nail and made him snatch his hand back. Suddenly he understood: that hand had not come to seize him, but to know him — to know this man, to know the guilty heart of his half-life, to know that every matter he had thrown down was still kept well at the bottom, not one missing.

At dawn there was nothing on the rim but moss thicker than the day before, reek heavier, as if that one hand had brought up a layer of the bottom's damp. Shen dared not sit by the well again; he took the polished rope indoors and locked the door. Yet he knew: the man below had finished reciting his three old cases, and stretched out his hand — this was not finished. The well that opens to the underworld has a longer memory than any man; what it has recorded needs no urging to be turned back.

From that night Shen aged ten years. He still locked the rim each day, still came out to sit at night, only he no longer dared lay his ear to the wall. He added another lock to the well, and another; the lock-tongues all bore the print of his grip, yet he knew clearly that locks could hold the living but not the one below who recited old accounts. Sometimes he woke startled at midnight to the well-rope creaking in the wind in the yard; plainly an empty well, yet it was as if someone lifted a bucket, once and again, to haul back up, one by one, the things he had thrown down across the years. He dared not answer, dared not look, only buried his head in the quilt and waited for dawn.

Every moonless night after, Shen heard the man below recite his affairs from the start again. And at the end, that gray-white hand would rest upon the rim once more, palm up, waiting for him to come down.

Note of the Midnight Record: The well does not swallow sound; he who throws things in must at last throw himself in.
